summary: For ages 8-9: round whole numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line FIRST — mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits — then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule as a shortcut justified by the midpoint. Core worked example: 4,367 rounds to 4,370 (nearest 10), 4,400 (nearest 100), 4,000 (nearest 1000). Deliberately teach the halfway convention (half rounds up) and cascade/carry cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100). Includes a number-line manipulation activity, a consolidation assessment with targeted traps, and a static reference image as a scaffold.
misconceptions: Rounding by the wrong digit or to the wrong place (ignoring which place is the target).
Always rounding down (truncating) or always up.
Chained/successive rounding (rounding the ones then tens then…) instead of one decision.
Mishandling the halfway case or the cascade (4,970 to nearest 100 → 4,900 not 5,000).
Treating rounding as a rule with no sense of 'nearer to', so unable to check reasonableness.

activities.title: Number-line rounding bench: snap to the nearer multiple
steps: Place or drag the target number (e.g. 4,367) as a marker on a number line between its two bounding multiples — 4,300 and 4,400 when rounding to the nearest 100 — with the midpoint 4,350 clearly flagged.
See that 4,367 sits PAST the midpoint, so it is nearer to 4,400; watch the marker snap to 4,400 (an arc or snap animation makes the 'nearer multiple' choice visible rather than recited).

Drag the marker back and forth across the midpoint and watch the rounded result flip at 4,350: whole numbers below 4,350 (e.g. 4,349) round down to 4,300, while 4,350 itself and anything above round up to 4,400. This shows that the midpoint is the tipping point, and that the half-rounds-up convention decides the exact-halfway case.
Use a target-place selector (10/100/1000) that rescales the line and changes the bounding multiples, so you feel how the target place chooses which multiples bound the number.
Work a cascade case: round 4,970 to the nearest 100 and watch the roll up to 5,000 — the hundreds carry over (49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000).
After the line meaning is built, name the 'decider' digit — the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to — and connect it to which side of the midpoint you are on.
activities.insight: Rounding means choosing the nearer multiple of the target place; the midpoint is the tipping point, and the 'look at the next digit' rule is just a quick way of telling whether the number is below halfway (decider 0-4, round down) or at or past halfway (decider 5-9, round up, with exactly halfway going up by the agreed convention).

activities.title: Consolidation across places with targeted traps
steps: Round given numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 (e.g. round 4,367 to each place) via fill-in or multiple choice.
First select the target place, then round, so the two steps stay distinct.
Tackle deliberately chosen trap cases: the halfway case 2,650 to the nearest 100 (which rounds up to 2,700), and the cascade case 1,970 to the nearest 100 (which carries to 2,000).
Match numbers to their rounded values across places.
activities.insight: Rounding can be applied reliably across different target places, including the halfway (5) and nine-cascade cases, once the nearness meaning is secure.

activities.title: Rounding-hill reference image (scaffold)
steps: Use a static rounding-hill / number-line poster showing the two bounding multiples and the marked midpoint as a reference while rounding.
Optionally tap a number on the hill to watch it roll to the nearer multiple, with the midpoint marked, as a reminder of the nearness decision.
activities.insight: A visual 'hill' with a marked midpoint reminds learners that rounding goes to the nearer multiple and that the midpoint decides direction.

checkQuestion: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 4,367 to the nearest hundred. Now round 1,970 to the nearest hundred. Now round 2,650 to the nearest hundred.' Ask them to show it on a number line for at least one. Watch which digit they use to decide and what they do to the digits after it.
checkAnswer: 4,400; 2,000; 2,700 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the hundreds, then replacing all digits after the hundreds place with zero.
